Chapter 3: The Invention of Good and Evil
Everywhere you look, every society has its own stories—stories about heroes and villains, about what’s right, and what’s wrong.
These tales, they don’t just entertain us. They shape how we see the world, giving meaning to our choices and our everyday lives.
But let’s be honest—how often do we really stop to wonder where these ideas came from? Or why good and evil look the way they do in different cultures?
Picture a community where everyone agrees—everyone is on the same page about what’s good and what’s evil. The rules are crystal clear.
If you follow them, you’re rewarded with respect, maybe even a sense of security. Sounds simple, right?
But underneath that surface, there’s tension. Some folks feel trapped by all those rules, while others turn the rules into a way to control or even dominate their neighbors.
Here’s something to pay attention to: the difference between good and evil isn’t a law of nature. It’s something people came up with—a tool for keeping order, making sense of things, and, sometimes, justifying the actions of those in charge.
Morality’s rules aren’t the same everywhere. They’re shaped by history, by the needs and ambitions of different groups and generations.
Now, imagine someone in that community starts to ask questions. Why is this action called good, but that one evil? Who really benefits from drawing these lines?
The answers aren’t always clear. In fact, sometimes what’s labeled as good is just what helps those in power, and what’s called evil is anything that threatens their hold.
As years go by, the rules get stricter. Question them, and you get punished. The difference between good and evil becomes automatic, just habit. People forget why the rules were there in the first place—and before you know it, the rules themselves become sacred, beyond question.
But here’s the thing: that divide between good and evil? It’s never set in stone. In every society, there’s always someone who refuses to just go along.
They realize morality isn’t about eternal truths—it’s about choices people have made, often to serve particular interests. And if people made the rules, people can change them.
So, what’s the real challenge? It’s not about clinging to the old lines between good and evil. It’s about having the courage to question them.
Only by challenging the rules can we create new ways of living—ways that are more creative, more honest, and truly life-affirming.
